narrative: Fire and climate dominate today's most striking findings: a review of Australia's 2019/2020 Black Summer response shows biodiversity protection can be integrated into emergency management even amid megafires, while multi-decadal evidence from the Pantanal links hydroclimatic disruption to longer, more intense fire seasons. On the movement and behaviour fronts, polar bears at the southern edge of their range show fine-scale spatial segregation tied to sea-ice persistence, and a global meta-analysis finds urban populations, especially birds, consistently bolder and more exploratory than their rural counterparts. Trophic ecology work is unusually strong this cycle: biological invasions are shown to disrupt size-spectrum and predator-prey mass relationships in freshwater fish communities, a new superposition method offers a faster route to reconstructing food webs from stable isotope data, and giant Japanese salamanders turn out to reshape trophic structure disproportionately to their rarity. Invasion biology contributes evidence that alien species can facilitate one another via reduced litter allelochemicals, supporting the invasional meltdown hypothesis, while a rangeland study finds that reducing livestock losses to carnivores can inadvertently reshape grazing pressure and land use. In conservation, 38 years of fen rewetting in Germany show vegetation recovery trending toward near-natural composition, and a Chinese case study finds mammal communities recovering from an extreme ice storm faster once poaching was curtailed. Methods development remains concentrated in bioacoustics, with a new evolutionary algorithm and a CLAP-based zero-shot classifier both aimed at scaling passive monitoring for wildlife. Finally, comparative genomics reveals structural variation underlying fungicide insensitivity in a barley pathogen, and a fern-versus-angiosperm genome comparison highlights strikingly divergent evolutionary trajectories between the two lineages.
